blocks.prompt: The River of Ice
blocks.text: A glacier begins with snow. Snow falls on a cold mountain. Some of it melts in the summer, but not all of it. The next winter, more snow falls on top. The old snow gets squashed underneath. It gets squashed for years and years. The air is pushed out of it. The snow turns hard, and it turns blue. Now it is glacier ice. The pile of ice gets very heavy. Heavy things do not sit still. The ice starts to slide down the mountain. It slides slower than a snail. It pushes rocks along as it goes. A glacier is a river made of ice.

blocks.prompt: A River You Cannot Watch Move
blocks.text: A river of water can reach the sea in a day. A river of ice needs a hundred years. That is what a glacier is: a river made of ice, moving too slowly for your eyes to catch. Every glacier starts as snow. Snow falls on a cold mountain. Summer melts some of it away. But if more snow falls in winter than melts in summer, the pile never disappears. It grows. Each new layer presses down on the layers below it and squeezes out the air. After many years, the soft snow becomes ice so packed and so dense that it looks blue. Then the pile gets heavy, and heavy things do not stay put. The ice near the bottom starts to squash sideways and creep downhill. The whole glacier flows. Most glaciers move only a few inches a day. A few in Greenland can travel more than a hundred feet in a single day. The ice does not go alone. It grabs rocks and drags them along the ground beneath it, and those rocks scrape the bedrock like sandpaper. Long after the ice is gone, you can still find the scratches.

the air has been squeezed out of it, so it is packed and dense
the pile gets so heavy that the ice at the bottom squashes sideways and creeps downhill
(inference: the rocks it dragged left scratches on the bedrock)

blocks.prompt: How a Snowflake Becomes a Mountain
blocks.text: Nothing about a snowflake suggests power. It weighs almost nothing. It melts on your glove. But stack enough snowflakes in a cold enough place, and they will carve a valley. A glacier gets built the same way every time. Snow falls on high ground. Summer arrives and melts some of it, but not all. The leftover snow waits, and the next winter buries it. Under the weight of the new snow, the old flakes lose their delicate points and pack into grainy pellets called firn. More winters pile on. The air gets squeezed out. After decades, the firn fuses into glacier ice, so dense that it glows blue. Then physics takes over. Ice is stubborn in small amounts and surprisingly soft in large ones. Once the pile is deep enough, the ice at the bottom begins to deform under the weight above it and creeps downhill. Meltwater underneath can help the whole slab slide. The top of the glacier does not bend. It is too cold and too brittle, so it cracks instead, splitting into deep gaps called crevasses as it rides along on the flowing ice below. A moving glacier does not just travel. It rips boulders out of the ground, carries them frozen into its underside, and uses them to sand the rock beneath. That is how a narrow mountain valley, cut by a river into a V, gets widened into a broad U. When the ice finally melts, it drops everything it was carrying in long ridges of rock and grit called moraines. The glacier disappears. The evidence does not.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Glaciers hold about two thirds of Earth's fresh water
Ice cores hold real air from 800,000 years ago

Accumulation zone on top, ablation zone below
About 2 billion people drink from glacier fed rivers

blocks.prompt: The Ice That Remembers
blocks.text: Ice keeps records better than almost anything else on Earth. Here is why. A glacier is built out of snowfall, one winter at a time. Snow is not solid. It is mostly air, and when the next winter's snow presses down on it, that air does not all escape. Some of it gets trapped in bubbles and sealed inside the ice, and there it stays. Every layer of a glacier holds a sample of the sky from the year it fell. Scientists drill down through the ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland and pull up long cylinders called cores. Reading a core is a little like reading tree rings. The layers stack in order, oldest at the bottom, and each one can be dated. Then the bubbles are cracked open in a laboratory and measured. Cores drilled in Antarctica have handed researchers actual air from eight hundred thousand years ago. Not a model of that air. The air. Ice preserves other things too. In 1991, hikers in the Alps found a man melting out of a glacier. He carried a copper axe and wore a bearskin hat, and there was an arrowhead buried in his shoulder. He had been frozen for roughly five thousand three hundred years, and he came out so well preserved that scientists could work out what he had eaten for his last meal. Whether a glacier grows or shrinks comes down to plain accounting. Snow arrives at the top, in what scientists call the accumulation zone. Ice melts away at the bottom, in the ablation zone. If the arriving beats the melting, the glacier thickens and pushes forward. If the melting wins, the glacier thins and its front retreats uphill. Right now the melting is winning almost everywhere. Glacier National Park in Montana held about one hundred and fifty glaciers in the middle of the 1800s. Roughly two dozen are still big enough to count. That matters beyond the scenery. Mountain glaciers work as frozen reservoirs. They lock water up as ice in the cold season and release it slowly through the warm one, feeding rivers that people farm with and drink from long after the last rain fell. About two billion people depend on water that starts as mountain ice. When the ice is gone, the river does not simply carry on. The tap runs hard for a while, and then it runs dry.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: About 10 percent of Earth's land sits under glacial ice
Antarctic ice is nearly 3 miles thick in places
Ice below about 150 feet flows instead of cracking
Long Island is rubble left by the last ice age
Canada is still rising now that the ice is gone
Jakobshavn Isbrae is among the fastest glaciers on Earth

blocks.prompt: The Slowest River on Earth
blocks.text: Stand on a glacier and nothing appears to happen. That is the trick. A glacier is a river, and like every river it is running downhill right now, under your boots, at a speed your eyes were never built to detect. It begins as snowfall on high, cold ground. A snowflake that lands and survives the summer is the start of everything. The next winter buries it, and the winter after that buries the burial. Under the growing weight the flakes lose their delicate arms, pack together into grainy pellets called firn, and finally fuse into solid ice with nearly all the air squeezed out of them. Ordinary ice looks clear. Glacial ice, compressed for centuries, absorbs the red end of sunlight and hands back the blue, which is why the inside of a crevasse glows like a swimming pool. Weight is what turns a snowfield into a glacier. Ice under enough pressure stops behaving like a solid and starts behaving like extremely stiff syrup. The crystals slip past one another, the mass deforms, and the whole thing creeps downslope. Meltwater at the base can lubricate the rock and let the glacier slide outright. The top hundred and fifty feet or so stay cold and brittle, riding along on the flowing ice beneath, and because brittle things cannot bend, that upper layer tears open into the deep cracks called crevasses. Most glaciers advance a few inches a day. Jakobshavn Isbrae in Greenland has been clocked at over a hundred feet a day, which for ice is a sprint. A glacier is also a machine for rearranging the world. It plucks boulders from the bedrock, freezes them into its underside, and drags them along as teeth. Those teeth grind a valley from a river's narrow V into a wide U. They polish stone and leave parallel scratches pointing the way the ice went. Everything the glacier carries gets dumped where it finally melts, in long ridges of rubble called moraines. Twenty thousand years ago, ice up to two miles deep lay over most of Canada and reached down into the United States. Long Island is a rubble pile it left behind. The scratches it cut are still visible on bare rock in Central Park. The land itself is still recovering. Ice that heavy pressed the crust down into the softer rock below, and now that the weight is gone, parts of Canada and Scandinavia are rising again, roughly half an inch a year, like a mattress after you get up. And glaciers keep records. Every layer of snow seals tiny bubbles of the air that was there the day it fell. Drill down through an Antarctic ice sheet and you are drilling backward through time. Cores pulled from that ice have given scientists a direct sample of the atmosphere from eight hundred thousand years ago. No one had to guess. The air was simply there, waiting. That archive is not the only thing melting. Glaciers around the world are losing more ice each summer than they gain each winter, and about two billion people drink from rivers that mountain ice feeds. The slowest rivers on Earth turn out to be the ones we can least afford to lose.
